chunks.text: 2 Results 2.1 Multi-national development and evaluation datasets We assembled a multi-national dataset of digitized H&E biopsy whole-slide images (WSIs) and clinical data from 14 breast cancer cohorts spanning seven countries across North America, Latin America, Europe, and the Middle East ( Figure 1 b). Five cohorts from three countries (Gundersen, Omica, TransNEO [ 90 ] , Yale [ 33 ] and NYU; N = 1,080) were used for development and nine independent cohorts from five countries (Protege, UChicago [ 49 ] , Nexus [ 103 ] , Dordrecht, IMPRESS [ 50 ] , Jagiellonian, Shaare Zedek, Providence [ 8 ] , and Łódź; N = 1,412) for evaluation, spanning diverse molecular subtypes and geographies. Of the development cohorts, Omica, Gundersen, and NYU were used for cross-validation (hereafter cross-validation cohorts), and TransNEO and Yale for training only ( Section 4.7 ). Cohort characteristics are given in Table 1 . The evaluation set ( Table 2 ), used for all reported pCR performance estimates, had an overall pCR rate of 37.3% and a near-even split across the molecular subtypes (36.7% TNBC, 31.5% HR + + /HER2 − - , 30.8% HER2 + + ). The label used for model development and evaluation was pCR, assessed at surgery as the absence of residual invasive disease in both the breast and regional lymph nodes, consistent with the NeoSTEEP definition [ 65 ] ( Section 4.1 ). Where available, response was additionally characterized by residual cancer burden (RCB) class [ 101 ] , from RCB-0 (equivalent to pCR) to RCB-III (extensive residual disease), which we used only as an exploratory secondary endpoint. As the evaluation cohorts differ in size, subtype composition, and pCR rate ( Figure 1 b), performance is pooled with a random-effects model throughout ( Section 4.9 ). This heterogeneity reflects real population differences, enabling a stronger assessment of generalizability.

In total, the imaging data comprise 3,606 pre-treatment biopsy slides carrying 19.6 million 224 × \times 224-pixel tissue patches (median 4,123 per slide; Figure 1 c). The overall sample size of our study substantially exceeds that of most previously reported histopathology-based NAT response prediction studies [ 90 , 2 , 50 , 32 , 75 ] . 2.2 NEO: a multi-modal AI model for predicting neoadjuvant therapy response We developed NEO ( Figures 1 and 4.2 ), a multi-modal AI model that integrates routine pre-treatment biopsy H&E WSIs and baseline clinical variables to estimate the probability of achieving pCR. The model operates in two steps. First, MORPHEUS infers expression values for 14,773 protein-coding genes from the WSIs, referred to here as H&E-inferred expression ( Figure 1 e). Falcon [ 10 ] , a pathology foundation model trained by self-supervised learning, extracts a morphological embedding for every 224 × \times 224-pixel patch. A model trained on paired H&E and bulk RNA sequencing data from TCGA then aggregates these embeddings over the slide by multiple-instance learning (MIL) into expression values. Second, the H&E-inferred expression is compressed to five components ( Section 4.6 ) and combined with baseline clinical variables ( Section 4.1 ) to produce a calibrated probability of pCR ( Figure 1 f). This is the only step trained on response data: explainable boosting machines (EBMs) [ 74 , 16 ] and tabular ResNets [ 42 ] were fitted on the 1,080 development patients, calibrated post hoc ( Section A.2.11 ), and ensembled ( Section 4.8 ). 2.3 External evaluation and benchmarking of NEO We evaluated NEO on nine independent external cohorts comprising 1,412 patients ( Figure 2 ).

NEO achieved a pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.792 (95% CI, 0.732–0.852; p = 3.4 × 10 − 6 p=3.4\times 10^{-6} versus a null AUROC of 0.5), with substantial heterogeneity across cohorts ( I 2 I^{2} = 74%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0.0040; both defined in Section A.3 ). Discrimination was above chance in every cohort: per-cohort AUROCs ranged from 0.658 to 0.880, and all 95% confidence intervals excluded 0.5 ( Figure 1 ). Discrimination held within each molecular subtype ( Figure 2 a): 0.699 (95% CI, 0.643–0.755; I 2 I^{2} = 0%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0; seven cohorts) for TNBC, 0.669 (0.576–0.763; I 2 I^{2} = 58%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0.0077; eight cohorts) for HER2 + + , and 0.762 (0.686–0.837; I 2 I^{2} = 0%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0; six cohorts) for HR + + /HER2 − - disease, each pooled over the cohorts with sufficient samples of that subtype ( Section 4.9 ; per-cohort estimates in Figure 1 b–d). We next assessed calibration, the agreement between predicted and observed pCR rates ( Figure 2 b, Section 4.10 ). The calibration slope did not differ significantly from 1 in any stratum (all patients: 1.11, 95% CI, 0.97–1.25; TNBC: 1.21, 95% CI, 0.89–1.52; HER2 + + : 0.75, 95% CI, 0.47–1.04; HR + + /HER2 − - : 1.17, 95% CI, 0.84–1.51), consistent with appropriately dispersed predictions. The intercept indicated under-prediction overall (0.18, 95% CI, 0.06–0.30) and in HER2 + + disease (0.36, 95% CI, 0.16–0.56) and did not differ significantly from zero in TNBC (0.13, 95% CI, -0.05–0.32) and HR + + /HER2 − - disease (-0.06, 95% CI, -0.35–0.23). To assess whether NEO does not merely restate the clinical variables available at diagnosis, we fitted a Firth-penalized logistic regression of pCR on the score within each cohort, adjusted for baseline clinical variables NEO consumes ( Section 4.1 ) together with histologic grade, and pooled the log odds ratios ( Figure 2 c, Section 4.11 ). Among complete cases (1,031 of the 1,412 patients, seven cohorts), the NEO score remained associated with pCR, with a pooled odds ratio of 1.46 per 0.1-unit increase (95% CI, 1.12–1.89; p = 0.013 p=0.013 ; I 2 I^{2} = 31%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0.020), so it carries information the clinical variables do not. We next benchmarked NEO against four computational TIL biomarkers ( Figure 2 d): computational tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (cTILs), the lymphocytes-to-tumor ratio (LTR), the inflamed tumor ratio (ITR) [ 2 ] , and muTILs [ 66 ] . We re-implemented the first three from their published definitions and ran muTILs with the authors’ released models ( Section A.4 ). On IMPRESS, our cTILs implementation reproduced the published results, whereas we were not able to reproduce the results reported for LTR and ITR ( Table 6 ). These methods score a slide only when their models detect the tissue compartments required by the metric, which failed on 108 of the 2,489 evaluation slides. The comparison therefore uses the shared-slide set, the 1,386 of 1,412 patients scored by all five methods ( Section A.4.5 ). NEO reached a pooled AUROC of 0.791 (95% CI, 0.732–0.850) against 0.516–0.583 for the four biomarkers. NEO’s advantage, expressed as the pooled paired AUROC difference, ranged from + 0.192 +0.192 AUROC over cTILs to + 0.279 +0.279 over ITR, all p < 5 × 10 − 4 p<5\times 10^{-4} ( Figure 2 a–d). Within subtypes, all twelve paired differences directionally favored NEO and eleven reached p < 0.05 p<0.05 .

The exception was NEO versus ITR for TNBC patients ( + 0.075 +0.075 , 95% CI, − 0.001 -0.001 – 0.152 0.152 ; p = 0.052 p=0.052 ; Figure 3 ). Against pathologist-assessed Ki-67, recorded in three cohorts for 237 patients, NEO reached 0.868 (95% CI, 0.821–0.914) versus 0.648 (95% CI, 0.591–0.706), a paired difference of + 0.216 +0.216 (95% CI, + 0.115 +0.115 – + 0.317 +0.317 ; p = 0.012 p=0.012 ; Figure 2 e; Figure 2 e). To assess whether NEO captures gradations of response beyond binary pCR, we also evaluated the same score against RCB class in the 361 patients across four cohorts with recorded RCB (inclusion criteria in Section 4.9 ). The NEO score decreased across increasing RCB from RCB-0 to RCB-III, with medians of 0.486, 0.312, 0.259, and 0.139 ( p = 4.2 × 10 − 25 p=4.2\times 10^{-25} , one-sided cohort-stratified Jonckheere–Terpstra test; Section A.7.1 ). It also separated RCB-0/I from RCB-II/III (AUROC 0.792, 95% CI, 0.656–0.928; Figure 4 b). Finally, the same score also ranked nodal response, without retraining, in the 536 clinically node-positive patients across six cohorts with determinable nodal outcomes (pooled AUROC 0.736, 95% CI, 0.644–0.829; Section A.7.2 ). For context, AUROC for overall pCR was 0.775 (95% CI, 0.632–0.918) in the same 536 patients. Both secondary endpoints overlap with the primary one: RCB-0 is pCR by definition, and an overall pCR implies nodal pCR, so neither contrast is fully independent of the primary result. We regard both as exploratory, as RCB was assessed for only a quarter of the evaluation patients and the nodal outcome is non-randomly missing for 16% of clinically node-positive patients. Taken together, NEO discriminated pCR in every evaluation cohort and molecular subtype, added information beyond the standard clinical variables, and outperformed the computational TIL biomarkers and Ki-67 on the same patients.

2.4 MORPHEUS: H&E-inferred expression recovers biologically meaningful programs The information passed to NEO from the biopsy slide is purely mediated via H&E-inferred gene expression, so what it can learn about tumor biology is bounded by what that expression captures. Here, we examined how faithfully gene expression is inferred, which biological programs are recovered, and whether the inferred expression is spatially and morphologically grounded in the tissue. MORPHEUS was developed on paired H&E and bulk RNA-seq from 32 TCGA projects, comprising 8,742 patients and 10,520 slides. We used a subset of this TCGA cohort (n = 1,748 patients) as the validation set, and the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) [ 30 ] cohort (n = 1,473 patients, providing 1,566 primary-tumor samples across 10 cancer types) as an evaluation cohort ( Figure 1 d; Tables 3 and 4 ). We define fidelity as the per-gene Pearson correlation r r between inferred and measured expression within each cancer type ( Section 4.12 ). On the TCGA validation subset the mean per-type median r r was 0.27 (range 0.16–0.39) across the 23 projects with at least 20 validation patients, rising to 0.59 (0.44–0.76) over each type’s 1,000 best-predicted genes ( Figure 5 ). That subset of TCGA also drove model selection, so these values are likely optimistic. In evaluation on CPTAC cases, the corresponding values were 0.20 (0.13–0.25) and 0.52 (0.44–0.60), with every cohort above zero. Thus, expression is recovered in every cancer type and transfers to data never seen during training or validation. Next, we asked whether certain gene expression pathways are more or less learnable from morphology. For example, TILs are known to be readily readable from pathology images by human [ 89 ] and rule-based computer systems [ 2 , 66 ] , so we might expect associated gene expression pathways to be readily encoded by MORPHEUS.

We performed a transcriptome-wide analysis for each of 23 TCGA cancer types, first ranking genes from high to low accuracy of inferred gene expression, which was used as input to gene set enrichment analysis ( Figure 3 a; Section 4.13 ). Several pathways were commonly enriched across multiple cancer types (adjusted p < 0.05 p<0.05 ): immune pathways, including allograft rejection (21 cancer types), interferon gamma response (19), IL6–JAK–STAT3 signaling (17) and inflammatory response (17); stromal pathways, including epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT; 19), apical junction (16) and coagulation (15). Within cancer types, tissue-specific patterns of enrichment were also observed. Proliferation pathways — including E2F targets and the G2M checkpoint — were enriched in 14 cancer types, consistent with mitotic activity being a grading feature at some sites and not others. In addition, estrogen response pathways reached significance in 6 cancer types, with a highly significant signal in breast (adjusted p < 0.002 p<0.002 ). As a sanity check, we asked whether the morphological correlates of the inferred expression were discernible on the corresponding H&E slide. We randomly sampled 100 H&E image patches per slide from the Jagiellonian cohort, a representative cohort from the evaluation set, and applied MORPHEUS to score each patch by the mean H&E-inferred expression of each gene expression pathway. We focused on three gene expression pathways (EMT, angiogenesis, and mitotic spindle) which may have morphological correlates, and asked two board-certified pathologists with subspecialty expertise in breast pathology to review the highest- and lowest-scoring patches ( Figure 3 b; Section 4.13 ).

For EMT, both reviewers found the contrast consistent with the program: the high-scoring patches contained cells that were more mesenchymal in appearance and predominantly stromal; the low-scoring patches contained cells that displayed more epithelioid and carcinoma-like features. For angiogenesis, vessels were identified in the high-scoring set, with none seen in the low-scoring set. Similarly, for mitotic spindle, high-scoring patches exhibited several mitotic figures, with none visible in the low-scoring set. Lastly, we subjected MORPHEUS to a more stringent test, asking whether predictions learned at the bulk tumor level recapitulated expression measured at patch-level resolution by spatial transcriptomics. The imaging-based platforms used here localize individual transcripts from a targeted gene list, so the transcripts of a given gene detected within a patch can be counted and set against the value inferred for that same patch. We used two publicly available breast cancer spatial transcriptomics datasets, one Xenium v1 [ 54 ] and one Xenium Prime 5K ( Figure 3 c; Section A.6.2 ). Neither slide is in TCGA, and both were profiled with a different assay from the bulk RNA-seq used in training. MORPHEUS was applied zero-shot — without retraining, fine-tuning, or spatial supervision of any kind — focusing on the highest fidelity pathways. We evaluated at the gene-level, with each gene drawn from the members driving its set’s enrichment in Figure 3 a. For TAGLN , a myofibroblast marker in the EMT set, the inferred and measured maps were positively correlated (Spearman ρ = + 0.54 \rho=+0.54 across the 3,614 patches of the Xenium v1 slide).

The same held for IL7R , a lymphocyte surface receptor in the inflammatory response set ( ρ = + 0.65 \rho=+0.65 across the 8,068 patches of the Xenium Prime slide). In these examples, patch-level predictions of MORPHEUS track spatial variation within a slide. Collectively, these data indicate that the H&E-inferred gene expression is quantitatively faithful across tumor types, recovering biologically coherent immune, stromal, and proliferative pathways; that it aligns with what human experts see; and that, for the genes and sections examined, patch-level predictions track measured spatial variation in gene expression. 2.5 Integration of H&E-inferred expression in pCR prediction: performance, explainability, and design NEO predicts pCR through H&E-inferred expression rather than directly from the image. That intermediate step yields a set of expression values for named genes, so, unlike an image embedding, it can be interpreted directly, and its composition can be chosen: which genes the model is given, and how compactly they are summarized, are design decisions rather than assay constraints. Here, we examined what this design provides: whether it improves discrimination ( Figure 4 a), what it reveals about the biology behind each prediction ( Figure 4 b, Figure 6 ), and how performance depends on the genes supplied and on the size of the summary ( Figure 4 c, d). We first tested whether that intermediate step improves discrimination. We refer to models that predict pCR from H&E-inferred expression as transcriptome-informed. For comparison, we trained MIL models that predict pCR directly from the foundation-model embeddings MORPHEUS takes as input. We refer to these as direct pCR prediction models. We scored them on identical patients in all nine evaluation cohorts ( Figure 4 a; Section A.2.13 ). Transcriptome-informed and direct pCR prediction models were each trained in two settings: uni-modal, and with the clinical variables added ( Figure 2 ).

The comparison used NEO’s neural-network-based pCR prediction model rather than its full ensemble, matching the direct models in architecture family ( Section A.2.13 ). In the multi-modal setting in which NEO operates, the transcriptome-informed pCR prediction model reached a pooled AUROC of 0.785 (95% CI, 0.728–0.841) against 0.740 (95% CI, 0.692–0.788) for the direct pCR prediction model, with a pooled paired difference of + 0.038 +0.038 AUROC (95% CI, + 0.020 +0.020 – + 0.056 +0.056 ; p = 1.4 × 10 − 3 p=1.4\times 10^{-3} ; Figure 2 h). Without the clinical variables the ordering was the same but the difference was not statistically significant (0.697 versus 0.678; + 0.017 +0.017 , 95% CI, − 0.018 -0.018 – + 0.053 +0.053 ; p = 0.30 p=0.30 ; Figure 2 g). H&E-inferred expression also improved on the clinical variables by themselves (0.785 versus 0.746; + 0.028 +0.028 , 95% CI, + 0.009 +0.009 – + 0.047 +0.047 ; p = 9.6 × 10 − 3 p=9.6\times 10^{-3} ; Figure 2 f). The pCR prediction model consumes the H&E-inferred expression not gene by gene but as five independent components (ICs), MORPHEUS-IC0 to MORPHEUS-IC4, collectively the MORPHEUS-ICs. The H&E-inferred expression of a fixed set of 2,427 genes drawn from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) gene families [ 100 , 63 ] is reduced by independent component analysis (ICA), fitted once on the TCGA validation subset and then frozen ( Section 4.6 ). Because the H&E-inferred expression enters the model as five tabular components, its contribution to the prediction is inspectable with an EBM. In NEO’s EBM, the five MORPHEUS-ICs carried a group importance of 0.28 in log-odds units compared to 0.44 for the eight clinical variables combined, a ratio of 0.63.

Individually, MORPHEUS-IC2 and MORPHEUS-IC0 ranked third and fourth of thirteen input features respectively and both contributed nearly monotonically to the predicted log-odds of pCR, whereas the other three components were mostly flat ( Figure 4 b; Section A.6.1 ). We annotated MORPHEUS-IC2 and MORPHEUS-IC0 using gene set enrichment analysis over genes ranked by their weight within each component ( Figure 5 ; Section 4.13 ). We next examined molecular correlates of NEO predictions, relating the score to measured gene expression in the TCGA breast cancer cohort (TCGA-BRCA) ( Figure 6 ; Section A.6.4 ). These analyses used the full TCGA-BRCA cohort, since the validation subset alone (212 patients) was too small to estimate enrichment stably. No TCGA patient carried a pCR label or entered the training of the pCR prediction models, but because inferred expression may track measured expression more closely on MORPHEUS’s own training-set patients, the association strengths below may be somewhat overstated. Pathway analysis of NEO scores found proliferative programs (E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, MYC targets, and mitotic spindle) to be positively associated with predicted pCR probability, consistent with the greater chemosensitivity of highly proliferative tumors [ 99 ] ( Figure 6 a). Immune and inflammatory signaling (interferon alpha and gamma signaling, IL6-JAK-STAT3, and complement) was also positively associated with NEO scores, consistent with the immune-dependent mechanisms engaged by anti-HER2 antibodies, immune checkpoint blockade, and chemotherapy-induced immunogenic cell death. In contrast, both early and late estrogen response were negatively associated with NEO scores. This finding is consistent with the low pCR rates of ER-driven tumors [ 112 ] .

To characterize the tumor immune microenvironment, we performed immune cell-type signature enrichment using single-sample GSEA, scoring each tumor’s expression profile against the 23 immune signatures of Bindea et al. [9] , and tested each signature’s association with the NEO score. B cells, activated dendritic cells, and helper T cells were positively associated with NEO scores ( Figure 6 b). These associations are compatible with lymphoid immune activity. In contrast, tissue-resident cell types (including eosinophils and mast cells) were negatively associated with NEO score. Within PAM50 subtypes, NEO scores were highest in basal-like and HER2-enriched tumors and lowest in luminal A, reflecting the established hierarchy of pCR rates across molecular subtypes [ 76 , 99 ] ( Figure 6 c). We next asked how much of the transcriptome the response signal requires, and whether choosing genes deliberately improves on an unselected list. We trained EBMs on H&E-inferred expression alone, reduced to five MORPHEUS-ICs as in NEO ( Section 4.6 ), and for subsets ranging from 10 genes to the 14,773 genes MORPHEUS predicts. Subsets were chosen four ways: at random (25 draws per size), by MORPHEUS fidelity, by per-gene pCR discrimination on the cross-validation cohorts, and as published signatures ( Figure 4 c; Section A.5.1 ).

Figure 4 c should be interpreted for the trends across length of gene list and selection strategy rather than for differences between individual points. Two trends emerged from the random draws. As the gene list size grew, mean performance rose, from 0.661 at 10 genes to 0.688 at 1,000, against 0.689 at all 14,773 genes. The range in performance across draws also narrowed, from roughly 0.10 in AUROC at 10 genes to under 0.02 at 1,000. Of the 25 random 10-gene lists, 10 performed below 0.66 and the worst reached only 0.594, whereas every 1,000-gene draw fell within 0.679–0.699. Every random 1,000-gene draw thus had a pooled AUROC close to that of all 14,773 genes, whichever genes it happened to contain. Deliberate selection might be expected to improve on an unselected gene list. For example, the 10 genes most associated with pCR on the cross-validation cohorts are AIM2 , GZMB , APOBEC3A , LAMP3 , TNIP3 , CTLA4 , ADAMDEC1 , CYB5R4 , TAP2 , and APOL4 , most of which are immune-related. Yet, these strategies showed no consistent advantage over random selection across gene list sizes. Ranking by per-gene pCR discrimination reached 0.684 with only 10 genes but changed little thereafter (0.679 at 1,000), and ranking by MORPHEUS fidelity fell below every random draw at 1,000 genes (0.668). The nine published signatures spanned 0.648 to 0.700, within the range of the random draws ( Figure 4 c). NEO’s 2,427-gene MSigDB-family gene list is of the broad kind these trends favor, and its genes were no more correlated with one another than those of a random draw of its size (mean absolute pairwise correlation 0.254; Figure 4 ). NEO’s gene list was fixed before these experiments ( Section 4.6 ), which did not inform its choice. Finally, we examined the other design parameter: the number of components the gene list is reduced to. We fixed this at five during development, where it gave the best validation performance.

A post hoc sweep on the evaluation cohorts is consistent with this choice: with clinical variables, pooled AUROC declines as the representation grows beyond five components, for all three reduction methods tested—ICA, PCA and sparse PCA ( Figure 4 d). The three methods performed comparably at five components; we chose ICA because it targets statistically independent components, a property suited to interpreting them individually. Together, these results indicate that prediction through H&E-inferred gene expression outperforms direct prediction from the same embeddings in the multi-modal setting and adds information beyond clinical variables alone. The representation is explainable, and its biology matches the established correlates of neoadjuvant response. They also indicate how to parameterize that representation: a broad, heterogeneous gene list, reduced to a small number of components. No selection strategy showed a consistent advantage over random selection, and five components sufficed to carry the signal. 2.6 Robustness of NEO predictions to tumor sampling bias Intratumor heterogeneity gives rise to sampling bias, which can confound genomic assays by giving different results depending on which part of the tumor bulk is sampled [ 43 , 11 ] . The problem of sampling bias is particularly relevant to prediction of pCR, as needle biopsy typically samples less than 1% of the tumor bulk [ 64 ] . We therefore quantified how much a patient’s NEO prediction depends on which slide is used, and benchmarked the computational TIL biomarkers on the same tissue. For this experiment, we used the UChicago cohort which contributes the most slides per patient (289 patients, 1,269 slides; Figure 5 ). When NEO was applied to individual slides, predictions were highly consistent within patients ( Figure 5 a). Across the 247 patients with more than one slide (median 4 slides per patient, up to 15), the intraclass correlation coefficient ICC(1,1) was 0.934 (95% CI, 0.909–0.954).

As an illustration at the sub-slide level, we applied NEO separately to the individual biopsy cores of four example slides ( Figure 5 b). In each example the independently scored cores gave similar predictions, both to one another and to the whole-slide prediction. We then compared NEO against the computational TIL biomarkers using an established variance-decomposition metric [ 4 , 12 ] . The metric is W / T W/T , the fraction of a biomarker’s total variance attributable to tumor sampling when k k slides are averaged. W W is the within-patient variance of the biomarker across slides of the same tumor, B B the variance between patients, and T = W + B T=W+B the total. We take W / T ≤ 0.15 W/T\leq 0.15 as the stability threshold adopted in the original study ( Section 4.14 ). Across the 242 multi-slide patients within the shared-slide set, NEO met the stability threshold from a single slide ( W / T = 0.05 W/T=0.05 ). Every computational TIL biomarker required substantially more, from 2.5 slides for ITR to 5.8 for muTILs ( Figure 5 c). Noting that NEO’s clinical inputs are identical across a patient’s slides and contribute no within-patient variance, we repeated the analysis on an imaging-only variant ( Section 4.15 ). It required 1.4 slides, still fewer than any of the other biomarkers, so NEO was the most stable of the scores with and without its clinical inputs. Finally, in a descriptive analysis, we asked whether predictions remain stable when far less tissue is sampled. We randomly subsampled patches from the 70 evaluation slides containing at least 10,000 patches ( ≈ \approx 125 mm 2 of tissue) and re-ran the imaging-only model on each subset ( Section 4.15 ). Because the imaging-only model has no clinical inputs fixed across subsamples, any stability must come from the tissue-derived signal itself.

For each slide and subset size, we computed the absolute difference between each subsampled prediction and the all-patch prediction, divided by the all-patch prediction. We averaged this relative change across 30 random subsamples per slide, and then took the median of per-slide averages. Predictions remained stable even with substantial subsampling. This median relative change was 3.4% with 500 patches ( ≈ \approx 6 mm 2 ) and 0.8% with 5,000 patches, and remained below 5% at all subset sizes of 500 patches or more. Only at 50 patches ( ≈ \approx 0.6 mm 2 ) did the median relative change rise to 11% ( Figure 5 d). Together, these data indicate that NEO yields a stable estimate from a single needle biopsy slide, a vital condition for biopsy-based biomarkers that existing histopathological markers do not meet. The imaging-only variant also remained stable under patch subsampling, supporting robustness to limited tissue. The top axis gives the corresponding tissue area (0.0125 mm 2 per patch). 2.1 Multi-national development and evaluation datasets We assembled a multi-national dataset of digitized H&E biopsy whole-slide images (WSIs) and clinical data from 14 breast cancer cohorts spanning seven countries across North America, Latin America, Europe, and the Middle East ( Figure 1 b). Five cohorts from three countries (Gundersen, Omica, TransNEO [ 90 ] , Yale [ 33 ] and NYU; N = 1,080) were used for development and nine independent cohorts from five countries (Protege, UChicago [ 49 ] , Nexus [ 103 ] , Dordrecht, IMPRESS [ 50 ] , Jagiellonian, Shaare Zedek, Providence [ 8 ] , and Łódź; N = 1,412) for evaluation, spanning diverse molecular subtypes and geographies. Of the development cohorts, Omica, Gundersen, and NYU were used for cross-validation (hereafter cross-validation cohorts), and TransNEO and Yale for training only ( Section 4.7 ). Cohort characteristics are given in Table 1 .

The evaluation set ( Table 2 ), used for all reported pCR performance estimates, had an overall pCR rate of 37.3% and a near-even split across the molecular subtypes (36.7% TNBC, 31.5% HR + + /HER2 − - , 30.8% HER2 + + ). The label used for model development and evaluation was pCR, assessed at surgery as the absence of residual invasive disease in both the breast and regional lymph nodes, consistent with the NeoSTEEP definition [ 65 ] ( Section 4.1 ). Where available, response was additionally characterized by residual cancer burden (RCB) class [ 101 ] , from RCB-0 (equivalent to pCR) to RCB-III (extensive residual disease), which we used only as an exploratory secondary endpoint. As the evaluation cohorts differ in size, subtype composition, and pCR rate ( Figure 1 b), performance is pooled with a random-effects model throughout ( Section 4.9 ). This heterogeneity reflects real population differences, enabling a stronger assessment of generalizability. In total, the imaging data comprise 3,606 pre-treatment biopsy slides carrying 19.6 million 224 × \times 224-pixel tissue patches (median 4,123 per slide; Figure 1 c). The overall sample size of our study substantially exceeds that of most previously reported histopathology-based NAT response prediction studies [ 90 , 2 , 50 , 32 , 75 ] . 2.2 NEO: a multi-modal AI model for predicting neoadjuvant therapy response We developed NEO ( Figures 1 and 4.2 ), a multi-modal AI model that integrates routine pre-treatment biopsy H&E WSIs and baseline clinical variables to estimate the probability of achieving pCR. The model operates in two steps. First, MORPHEUS infers expression values for 14,773 protein-coding genes from the WSIs, referred to here as H&E-inferred expression ( Figure 1 e). Falcon [ 10 ] , a pathology foundation model trained by self-supervised learning, extracts a morphological embedding for every 224 × \times 224-pixel patch.

A model trained on paired H&E and bulk RNA sequencing data from TCGA then aggregates these embeddings over the slide by multiple-instance learning (MIL) into expression values. Second, the H&E-inferred expression is compressed to five components ( Section 4.6 ) and combined with baseline clinical variables ( Section 4.1 ) to produce a calibrated probability of pCR ( Figure 1 f). This is the only step trained on response data: explainable boosting machines (EBMs) [ 74 , 16 ] and tabular ResNets [ 42 ] were fitted on the 1,080 development patients, calibrated post hoc ( Section A.2.11 ), and ensembled ( Section 4.8 ). 2.3 External evaluation and benchmarking of NEO We evaluated NEO on nine independent external cohorts comprising 1,412 patients ( Figure 2 ). NEO achieved a pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.792 (95% CI, 0.732–0.852; p = 3.4 × 10 − 6 p=3.4\times 10^{-6} versus a null AUROC of 0.5), with substantial heterogeneity across cohorts ( I 2 I^{2} = 74%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0.0040; both defined in Section A.3 ). Discrimination was above chance in every cohort: per-cohort AUROCs ranged from 0.658 to 0.880, and all 95% confidence intervals excluded 0.5 ( Figure 1 ). Discrimination held within each molecular subtype ( Figure 2 a): 0.699 (95% CI, 0.643–0.755; I 2 I^{2} = 0%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0; seven cohorts) for TNBC, 0.669 (0.576–0.763; I 2 I^{2} = 58%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0.0077; eight cohorts) for HER2 + + , and 0.762 (0.686–0.837; I 2 I^{2} = 0%, τ 2 \tau^{2} = 0; six cohorts) for HR + + /HER2 − - disease, each pooled over the cohorts with sufficient samples of that subtype ( Section 4.9 ; per-cohort estimates in Figure 1 b–d). We next assessed calibration, the agreement between predicted and observed pCR rates ( Figure 2 b, Section 4.10 ).

The calibration slope did not differ significantly from 1 in any stratum (all patients: 1.11, 95% CI, 0.97–1.25; TNBC: 1.21, 95% CI, 0.89–1.52; HER2 + + : 0.75, 95% CI, 0.47–1.04; HR + + /HER2 − - : 1.17, 95% CI, 0.84–1.51), consistent with appropriately dispersed predictions. The intercept indicated under-prediction overall (0.18, 95% CI, 0.06–0.30) and in HER2 + + disease (0.36, 95% CI, 0.16–0.56) and did not differ significantly from zero in TNBC (0.13, 95% CI, -0.05–0.32) and HR + + /HER2 − - disease (-0.06, 95% CI, -0.35–0.23). We next benchmarked NEO against four computational TIL biomarkers ( Figure 2 d): computational tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (cTILs), the lymphocytes-to-tumor ratio (LTR), the inflamed tumor ratio (ITR) [ 2 ] , and muTILs [ 66 ] . We re-implemented the first three from their published definitions and ran muTILs with the authors’ released models ( Section A.4 ). On IMPRESS, our cTILs implementation reproduced the published results, whereas we were not able to reproduce the results reported for LTR and ITR ( Table 6 ). These methods score a slide only when their models detect the tissue compartments required by the metric, which failed on 108 of the 2,489 evaluation slides. The comparison therefore uses the shared-slide set, the 1,386 of 1,412 patients scored by all five methods ( Section A.4.5 ). NEO reached a pooled AUROC of 0.791 (95% CI, 0.732–0.850) against 0.516–0.583 for the four biomarkers. NEO’s advantage, expressed as the pooled paired AUROC difference, ranged from + 0.192 +0.192 AUROC over cTILs to + 0.279 +0.279 over ITR, all p < 5 × 10 − 4 p<5\times 10^{-4} ( Figure 2 a–d). Within subtypes, all twelve paired differences directionally favored NEO and eleven reached p < 0.05 p<0.05 . The exception was NEO versus ITR for TNBC patients ( + 0.075 +0.075 , 95% CI, − 0.001 -0.001 – 0.152 0.152 ; p = 0.052 p=0.052 ; Figure 3 ). Against pathologist-assessed Ki-67, recorded in three cohorts for 237 patients, NEO reached 0.868 (95% CI, 0.821–0.914) versus 0.648 (95% CI, 0.591–0.706), a paired difference of + 0.216 +0.216 (95% CI, + 0.115 +0.115 – + 0.317 +0.317 ; p = 0.012 p=0.012 ; Figure 2 e; Figure 2 e). To assess whether NEO captures gradations of response beyond binary pCR, we also evaluated the same score against RCB class in the 361 patients across four cohorts with recorded RCB (inclusion criteria in Section 4.9 ).

The NEO score decreased across increasing RCB from RCB-0 to RCB-III, with medians of 0.486, 0.312, 0.259, and 0.139 ( p = 4.2 × 10 − 25 p=4.2\times 10^{-25} , one-sided cohort-stratified Jonckheere–Terpstra test; Section A.7.1 ). It also separated RCB-0/I from RCB-II/III (AUROC 0.792, 95% CI, 0.656–0.928; Figure 4 b). Finally, the same score also ranked nodal response, without retraining, in the 536 clinically node-positive patients across six cohorts with determinable nodal outcomes (pooled AUROC 0.736, 95% CI, 0.644–0.829; Section A.7.2 ). For context, AUROC for overall pCR was 0.775 (95% CI, 0.632–0.918) in the same 536 patients. Both secondary endpoints overlap with the primary one: RCB-0 is pCR by definition, and an overall pCR implies nodal pCR, so neither contrast is fully independent of the primary result. We regard both as exploratory, as RCB was assessed for only a quarter of the evaluation patients and the nodal outcome is non-randomly missing for 16% of clinically node-positive patients. Taken together, NEO discriminated pCR in every evaluation cohort and molecular subtype, added information beyond the standard clinical variables, and outperformed the computational TIL biomarkers and Ki-67 on the same patients. 3 Discussion Neoadjuvant therapy commits a patient to months of systemic treatment before pathological response can be assessed at surgery. Its principal endpoint, pCR, is strongly associated with long-term outcomes [ 21 , 97 ] , and predicting pCR accurately offers the potential for de-escalation of chemotherapy [ 81 ] , alternative regimens, or trial enrollment. We developed NEO to estimate pCR from the two inputs already acquired at diagnosis—the biopsy H&E slide and the baseline clinical variables—adding no tissue, assay, or manual read to the workflow. Its first step, MORPHEUS, is a pan-cancer model inferring transcriptome-wide expression from morphology.

NEO then predicts pCR from the H&E-inferred gene expression together with the clinical variables. Across 1,412 patients from nine independent cohorts, NEO discriminated responders within the three molecular subtypes, and added information beyond the clinical variables already available at diagnosis. The prediction is also interpretable in terms of the molecular signal it uses. Rather than predicting pCR directly from an image embedding, NEO operates on five MORPHEUS-ICs, each a weighted combination of the 2,427-gene list. The two MORPHEUS-ICs the model relies on most contribute nearly monotonically to the predicted probability, and the five together carry just under two-thirds the group importance of the eight clinical variables ( Figure 4 b). Consistent with this dependence on transcriptomic features, NEO’s transcriptomic and immune-cell correlates are the established correlates of neoadjuvant response ( Figure 6 a,b). Grounding a prediction in established response biology, rather than in an opaque embedding, may ease its path to clinical adoption. These correlates recover the axes that a multi-omic characterization of the same endpoint identified. Previous analyses have profiled pre-treatment biopsies via DNA- and RNA-sequencing, together with digital pathology, finding that tumors attaining pCR were jointly high in proliferation and in immune activation [ 90 ] . Here, we reproduce this result ( Figure 6 a,b), notably only using the diagnostic H&E slide. No tool in routine clinical use supplies an estimate of pCR likelihood across breast cancer subtypes. Multigene assays measure small targeted lists and estimate recurrence risk rather than response to NAT [ 79 , 96 , 78 ] . HER2DX predicts pCR, but only in HER2 + + disease and only with an RNA assay [ 86 ] . Histopathological markers reproduce poorly [ 60 , 85 ] and are vulnerable to tumor sampling bias from needle biopsy [ 43 ] .

Machine-learning predictors of NAT response, including those that predict through inferred expression [ 48 , 14 ] , have meanwhile been trained on small cohorts with limited external validation [ 90 , 50 , 75 , 2 ] . NEO, by contrast, was developed on five multi-institutional cohorts and evaluated across nine. It outperformed the computational TIL biomarkers and pathologist-assessed Ki-67 and remained associated with pCR after adjustment for clinical variables. It is not confined to a targeted gene list either: inference supplies 14,773 genes from the slide alone. Breadth is also what removes the need to choose well. Small gene lists varied widely in performance depending on their composition, whereas larger random lists approached full-transcriptome performance more reliably ( Figure 4 c). One reason may be redundancy: ranked lists accumulate mutually correlated genes ( Figure 4 ), so growing such a gene list adds little new signal. Building a gene list from each gene’s association with pCR requires NAT labels and, when estimated on small cohorts, risks capturing spurious associations. Prediction fidelity also does not help — selecting the genes MORPHEUS infers most faithfully never beat random selection — so a wide, imprecisely inferred gene list is a better substrate than a narrow, accurately inferred one. This makes breadth a variance-reduction strategy, and one available without response labels. However, breadth of input did not require breadth of representation: pooled AUROC did not improve beyond five components ( Figure 4 d). A plausible explanation is that individual inferred gene values are noisy and that reducing the gene list to a few components averages that noise away while preserving the programs that carry response signal. A wider representation may also dilute the contribution of the clinical variables, which are few but individually strong.

NEO is also fully automated, which eliminates inter-observer variability by construction, and its prediction is stable under the biopsy sampling that confounds the histopathological markers. End to end, scoring a patient takes approximately five minutes on average on a single modern GPU, requiring no reagent or tissue beyond the diagnostic block. A needle core captures less than 1% of a heterogeneous tumor, which makes stability of predictions under sampling a prerequisite. NEO reached a stable estimate from a single slide, whereas computational TIL biomarkers required 2.5 to 5.8 slides ( Figure 5 c). Illustrative examples suggest the same at the sub-slide level. Independently scored cores of one slide gave similar predictions ( Figure 5 b), and the imaging-only prediction changed little under patch subsampling down to ≈ {\approx} 6 mm 2 of tissue ( Figure 5 d). NEO predictions are robust to tumor sampling bias, whether from spatial heterogeneity or from limited tissue quantity, remaining stable within the range of variation seen with pretreatment core biopsies. Prior work has established that gene expression may be learned from pathology slides [ 28 , 48 ] . Here, we expand on these efforts by establishing exactly which genomic programs are learnable from H&E slides, and whether this varies between cancer types. We discover that molecular signals of immune infiltration and stromal remodeling could be inferred from morphology in nearly every cancer type. In addition, tissue-specific signals were identified: proliferation pathways were detectable in cancer types where mitotic activity is part of routine grading; estrogen response was measurable most strongly in breast cancer, and also in other hormone-driven cancer types. Unlike previous work, we also confirm correspondence between predicted molecular signals and associated morphological features through annotation by board-certified pathologists with subspecialty expertise in breast cancer.

Several of these biological signals already inform computational or clinical approaches in pathology. TILs, which pathologists can identify on H&E slides, have already been the subject of numerous computational approaches [ 2 , 66 , 87 ] . The proliferation and hormone-driven features identified here have likewise been used in multivariable models predicting neoadjuvant chemotherapy response in ER + + /HER2 − - tumors [ 56 , 7 , 34 ] , although those models require reliable semiquantitative immunohistochemistry. By identifying which molecular programs can be inferred from morphology and in which cancer types, our findings may help prioritize biological targets and disease settings for future AI tools in pathology. Prior studies have also demonstrated the added utility of transcriptome-informed predictions from H&E slides for modeling treatment responses — versus direct pathology predictions — in a pan-cancer cohort [ 48 ] , and on small datasets with dozens of breast tumors [ 14 ] . Here, we extend these efforts by testing the hypothesized advantage of transcriptome-informed pCR prediction at scale: developed using 1,080 patients (five cohorts) and evaluated in 1,412 patients (nine cohorts). A plausible explanation is that MORPHEUS simplifies the learning problem by first compressing the image embeddings into biologically meaningful features. Developed on 8,742 TCGA patients to predict the expression of 14,773 genes, MORPHEUS learned to relate morphology to gene expression. The model trained on the NAT cohorts is then left with the simpler task of relating the inferred expression to response. In the direct pCR prediction model, morphology must be related directly to response from a thousand response labels. The strategy generalizes: pretrain the image-to-biology step on abundant paired data, then fit the clinical endpoint on the compact representation it yields, so that the endpoint model can be estimated from a modest cohort.

However, this strategy may not remain necessary as training data accumulate. With a cohort large enough to identify which morphology matters from response labels alone, we expect the advantage of the intermediate step to narrow. This study has limitations. First, the evaluation cohorts are observational, with patients treated according to local practice. They validate NEO as a predictor of pCR, however, based on the results presented in this study alone, cannot inform specific treatment decisions. This can be explored using data from clinical trials. The PHERGain trials used response-adapted strategies to omit chemotherapy in patients with HER2 + + early breast cancer who responded to neoadjuvant trastuzumab and pertuzumab alone, in both the randomized PHERGain trial [ 82 , 81 ] and the single-arm PHERGain-2 trial [ 40 ] . Our companion study validates NEO in these trials, finding that model predictions maintain performance in the setting of chemotherapy de-escalation [ 88 ] . Second, three of the four computational TIL biomarkers (cTILs, LTR and ITR) rest on our own re-implementation. We built them from the published definitions of Aswolinskiy et al. [2] with a different segmentation backbone because the reference implementation could not be obtained ( Section A.4 ). Although the original authors indicated that alternative segmentation backbones could be used, differences between our reproduced and published LTR and ITR performance warrant caution when interpreting these comparisons. muTILs, however, runs on the authors’ released models and performed no better, suggesting the computational TIL biomarkers’ limited discrimination is not solely due to re-implementation. Third, NEO was benchmarked only against pathology-based computational TIL biomarkers and Ki-67, as these were the sole benchmarks available in the NAT cohorts. Future work will compare performance against genomic assays.

Fourth, the tissue-sampling analysis ( Figure 5 d) subsampled patches at random from large slides rather than evaluating genuinely small specimens. Finally, both secondary endpoints are exploratory: RCB is sparsely assessed, and the nodal outcome is non-randomly missing. Future work could strengthen the learned representation at its source, for example by fine-tuning the pathology foundation model on the paired gene expression data or by including gene expression in its pretraining [ 104 , 55 , 80 ] . In addition, the bulk transcriptome-informed approach developed here may be extended to spatially resolved expression inference [ 94 ] , building on the zero-shot examples in Figure 3 c. With larger datasets, NEO could be extended with a causal module that predicts pCR under each candidate treatment while adjusting for non-random treatment allocation [ 10 ] . Beyond the retrospective data presented here, prospective evaluation is the necessary next step to establish clinical utility and impact on outcomes [ 12 ] . A silent-deployment study of NEO, in which the model runs prospectively without influencing care, is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07327970) and has begun enrollment. 4 Methods 4.1 Neoadjuvant cohorts and data To develop and evaluate a model for pre-treatment prediction of response to NAT, we assembled a multi-national dataset of H&E-stained breast cancer biopsy WSIs paired with baseline clinical variables and pCR outcomes.
